Constipation in children
Hard, painful or infrequent poo is common in children; most cases improve with diet and toilet habits.
Potty training, starting nursery and diet changes can trigger constipation.
After a painful poo the child starts holding it in, and constipation can become a vicious circle.
Poo leaking into underwear can also be a sign of constipation.
Increase vegetables, fruit, pulses and whole grains; don't forget water.
Build a routine of sitting on the toilet for 5–10 minutes after meals; put a step under their feet.
Encourage active play and time outdoors.
Don't use an enema or laxative without talking to a doctor.
Blood in the poo, severe tummy pain, vomiting or a swollen tummy.
If constipation lasts longer than 2 weeks or there is weight loss.
Constipation present since infancy.
Bedwetting (at night)
Night-time dryness develops later than daytime dryness; bedwetting is common up to age 5.
Bladder capacity and the hormone that reduces urine at night take time to mature.
A similar history in the family is common.
The child doesn't do it on purpose; punishment and shaming make it worse.
Reduce drinks after dinner but make sure they drink enough during the day.
Add going to the toilet before bed to the routine.
Put a waterproof cover on the bed; celebrate dry nights with a small calendar.
If it continues after age 7.
If it starts again after being dry for a long time.
If it comes with daytime accidents, burning when peeing, drinking a lot or peeing a lot.
Head lice
Head lice are common at nursery and school age; they're unrelated to cleanliness and can be treated.
Lice spread by head-to-head contact; they don't jump or fly.
Itching at the nape and behind the ears is the most common sign.
White eggs (nits) stuck near the scalp don't fall off easily, unlike dandruff.
Wet the hair, apply conditioner and comb strand by strand with a fine-toothed lice comb.
Use pharmacy lice treatments following the age limit and instructions on the box.
Repeat combing 7–10 days after treatment.
Check everyone at home; wash pillowcases in hot water.
For children under 2, talk to a doctor before using any treatment.
If itchy sores have become infected.
If lice persist despite correct treatment.
Screening tests in pregnancy
Screening tests estimate the likelihood of certain conditions in the baby; they don't give a definite diagnosis.
At weeks 11–14 the combined test and nuchal translucency scan may be done.
At weeks 18–22 a detailed ultrasound examines the baby's organs.
At weeks 24–28 a glucose tolerance test for gestational diabetes is recommended.
After a high-risk result, further tests may be offered for a definite diagnosis.
Add which tests are recommended for you, and when, to your checklist.
Review the result together with your doctor; don't interpret it alone.
Write your questions in the question notebook before the appointment.
If the result is “high risk”, discuss genetic counselling and further testing options.
Bleeding, fluid leaking, fever or severe pain after a test: see a doctor immediately.

Lower back and back pain in pregnancy
A growing bump, loosening ligaments and changing posture make back pain common in pregnancy.
Pain usually increases in the second and third trimesters.
Pain in the hips and at the front of the pelvis (symphysis) can also occur.
Regular, rhythmic back pain can be a sign of labour starting or preterm labour.
Don't lift heavy loads; bend your knees when bending down.
When lying on your side, put a pillow between your knees.
Wear flat, comfortable shoes.
Walking, pregnancy yoga and swimming can strengthen muscles; talk to your doctor before using painkillers.
If the pain comes rhythmically, or with bleeding or fluid leaking: see a doctor immediately.
If there is fever, burning when peeing or pain in the side.
If there is numbness or weakness in the legs.
Heartburn and constipation in pregnancy
Hormones and the growing womb slow digestion; heartburn and constipation are very common.
Heartburn gets worse especially after meals and when lying down.
Iron supplements can make constipation worse.
Constipation can lead to haemorrhoids.
Eat small, frequent meals; don't lie down for 2–3 hours after eating.
Cut down on spicy, fatty and acidic foods; raise your head when lying down.
Increase fibre-rich foods and water, and walk every day.
Use antacids or laxatives only after asking your doctor.
Severe pain in the upper stomach, headache and blurred vision (possible signs of pre-eclampsia): see a doctor immediately.
If you can't keep fluids down because of vomiting.
If there is blood in your poo.
Sleep and sleeping position in pregnancy
In later pregnancy lying on your side is recommended for both mother and baby.
After week 28, lying on your back for long can press on large blood vessels.
